notes:
Basic Definitions

  • Order = order of the highest derivative present. Degree = power of the highest order derivative, provided the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives; otherwise degree is not defined (e.g. when $\sin, \cos, e$ of a derivative appears).
  • A general solution has as many independent arbitrary constants as the order of the DE. A particular solution fixes those constants using given conditions, so it has zero arbitrary constants.

Formation of a Differential Equation

  • Given a family of curves with $n$ arbitrary constants, differentiate $n$ times and eliminate the constants to obtain a DE of order $n$.

Variable Separable

  • If the equation can be written as $g(y)\,dy = f(x)\,dx$, integrate both sides directly.

Homogeneous Differential Equations

  • $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$, a function of $y/x$ only. Substitute $y = vx$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$; this converts the equation to variable-separable form in $v$ and $x$.

Linear Differential Equations

Form$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ ($P,Q$ functions of $x$ only)
Integrating factor$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx}$
Solution$y\cdot(\text{I.F.}) = \displaystyle\int Q\cdot(\text{I.F.})\,dx + C$
Other form$\dfrac{dx}{dy} + P_1x = Q_1$, I.F. $= e^{\int P_1\,dy}$

Common Families and their DEs

  • Lines through origin $y=mx$ → $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y$.
  • Circles centred at origin $x^2+y^2=r^2$ → $x + y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 3–4 questions from this chapter: one on order/degree (often a 'degree not defined' trap), one on forming a DE from a given family, and one or two on solving a variable-separable, homogeneous, or linear DE. Practise finding the integrating factor quickly — it is the fastest way to identify the correct option.

questions.q: The order and degree of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3 = x$ are
questions.explanation: The highest order derivative present is $d^3y/dx^3$, so order $=3$; it occurs with power 2, so degree $=2$.
questions.trick: Order = highest derivative's order; degree = its power (must be polynomial).

questions.q: The degree of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \sin\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0$ is
questions.explanation: Since $\sin(dy/dx)$ is not a polynomial expression in the derivative, the degree of this (order 1) equation is not defined.
questions.trick: Trig or exp of a derivative $\Rightarrow$ degree not defined — spot it instantly.

questions.q: The number of arbitrary constants in the general solution of a differential equation of order 4 is
questions.explanation: A general solution of an $n$th order differential equation contains exactly $n$ independent arbitrary constants.
questions.trick: General solution's constant count always equals the order of the DE.

questions.q: The differential equation whose general solution is $y = A\cos 2x + B\sin 2x$ is
questions.explanation: Differentiating twice: $y'' = -4A\cos2x - 4B\sin2x = -4y$, so $y'' + 4y = 0$.
questions.trick: Differentiate twice: the squared coefficient inside $\cos/\sin$ becomes the DE's constant.

questions.q: Eliminating the arbitrary constant $r$ from the family of circles $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ gives the differential equation
questions.explanation: Differentiating $x^2+y^2=r^2$ w.r.t. $x$: $2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow x + y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$.
questions.trick: One constant to eliminate $\Rightarrow$ differentiate implicitly just once.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}$ is
questions.explanation: Separating variables, $\dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{dx}{x} \Rightarrow \ln|y| = \ln|x| + \ln C \Rightarrow y = Cx$.
questions.trick: $dy/y=dx/x$ separates instantly; the solution is always $y=Cx$.

questions.q: The solution curve of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}$ passing through $(1,2)$ meets the line $x=5$ at $y=$
questions.explanation: The family is $y=Cx$; at $(1,2)$, $C=2$, so $y=2x$. At $x=5$, $y=10$.
questions.trick: Find $C$ from the given point first, then plug in the target $x$.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x-y}$ is
questions.explanation: Rewrite as $e^y dy = e^x dx$ and integrate both sides: $e^y = e^x + C$.
questions.trick: Rewrite $e^{x-y}=e^x/e^y$, then separate as $e^y dy=e^x dx$.

questions.q: For the homogeneous equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x+y}{x}$, putting $y = vx$ reduces it to $x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = 1$. Hence $\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ equals
questions.explanation: With $y=vx$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$, so $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$, i.e. $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1/x$.
questions.trick: $y=vx$ turns $dy/dx$ into $v+x(dv/dx)$ — the standard first move.

questions.q: A differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$ is called
questions.explanation: By definition, such an equation, expressible as a function of $y/x$ alone, is a homogeneous differential equation.
questions.trick: A function of $y/x$ alone (degree-0 in $x,y$) is homogeneous.

questions.q: The integrating factor of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{y}{x} = x^2$ is
questions.explanation: Here $P=1/x$, so $\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx} = e^{\ln x} = x$.
questions.trick: I.F. $=e^{\int P\,dx}$; here $\int(1/x)dx=\ln x$ gives I.F.$=x$.

questions.q: Using the integrating factor $x$ (since $P=1/x$ gives $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int\frac{1}{x}dx}=x$), the general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{y}{x} = x^2$ is
questions.explanation: $y\cdot x = \int x^2\cdot x\,dx = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + C$, so $y = \dfrac{x^3}{4} + \dfrac{C}{x}$.
questions.trick: Multiply by the I.F., recognise LHS as $d/dx(y\cdot\text{I.F.})$, then integrate.

questions.q: The particular solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 1$ with $y(0) = 0$ is
questions.explanation: I.F. $=e^x$; $(ye^x)' = e^x \Rightarrow ye^x = e^x + C$. At $x=0,y=0$: $0=1+C \Rightarrow C=-1$, so $y=1-e^{-x}$.
questions.trick: Solve the general solution first, then use the initial condition to pin down $C$.

questions.q: If $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2xy}{1+x^2}$ and $y(0)=1$, then $y(1) =$
questions.explanation: Separating, $\dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}dx \Rightarrow \ln y = \ln(1+x^2)+C \Rightarrow y=A(1+x^2)$. Using $y(0)=1$ gives $A=1$, so $y=1+x^2$; $y(1)=2$.
questions.trick: Numerator is the derivative of the denominator $\Rightarrow$ separates straight to $\ln$.

questions.q: Eliminating the arbitrary constant $a$ from the family of parabolas $y^2 = 4ax$ gives the differential equation
questions.explanation: Differentiating, $2yy' = 4a \Rightarrow a = yy'/2$. Substituting back: $y^2 = 4x\left(\dfrac{yy'}{2}\right) = 2xyy' \Rightarrow y = 2xy'$ (dividing by $y$).
questions.trick: Differentiate once, solve for the constant, substitute it back into the original.

questions.q: An equation involving derivatives of the dependent variable with respect to only one independent variable is called
questions.explanation: By definition, a differential equation with derivatives taken with respect to a single independent variable is called ordinary (as opposed to partial).
questions.trick: One independent variable $\Rightarrow$ ordinary; more than one $\Rightarrow$ partial.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-x}{y}$ represents a family of
questions.explanation: Separating, $y\,dy = -x\,dx \Rightarrow \dfrac{y^2}{2} = -\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C \Rightarrow x^2+y^2 = 2C$, a family of concentric circles.
questions.trick: $y\,dy=-x\,dx$ integrates to a circle $x^2+y^2=\text{const}$.

questions.q: If $y = e^{mx}$ is a solution of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 5\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 6y = 0$, the possible values of $m$ are
questions.explanation: Substituting $y=e^{mx}$ gives $m^2 - 5m + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (m-2)(m-3)=0 \Rightarrow m=2,3$.
questions.trick: Substitute $y=e^{mx}$: turns the DE into a quadratic in $m$ (auxiliary equation).

questions.q: The order and degree of $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 + \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$ are
questions.explanation: The highest order derivative is $d^2y/dx^2$ (order 2), and it appears to the first power (degree 1).
questions.trick: Highest derivative present sets the order; its power sets the degree.

questions.q: The number of arbitrary constants present in the particular solution of a differential equation of order 3 is
questions.explanation: A particular solution is obtained by assigning specific values to all arbitrary constants using given conditions, leaving none free.
questions.trick: Particular solution: every constant gets evaluated, so zero remain free.

questions.q: The order and degree of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 + y = 0$ are
questions.explanation: The highest derivative present is $dy/dx$ (order 1), raised to the power 3 (degree 3).
questions.trick: Count the power on the single highest derivative present, for degree.

questions.q: The differential equation of the family of lines $y=mx+c$, where $m$ and $c$ are arbitrary constants, is
questions.explanation: Since there are two arbitrary constants, differentiate twice: $y'=m$ (constant), so $y''=0$.
questions.trick: Two constants $\Rightarrow$ differentiate twice to eliminate both, giving $y''=0$.

questions.q: The number of arbitrary constants in the general solution of a differential equation of order 2 is
questions.explanation: A general solution of an $n$th order DE has exactly $n$ arbitrary constants, so here $2$.
questions.trick: $n$ arbitrary constants for an $n$th-order general solution — direct rule.

questions.q: The order and degree of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+5\dfrac{dy}{dx}-6y=\log x$ are
questions.explanation: The highest order derivative is $d^2y/dx^2$ (order 2) and it appears to the first power (degree 1); $\log x$ is just a function of $x$, not of a derivative.
questions.trick: A pure function of $x$ (like $\log x$) never affects the degree.

questions.q: Eliminating the arbitrary constant $C$ from $y=Ce^{x}$ gives the differential equation
questions.explanation: Differentiating, $y'=Ce^x=y$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$.
questions.trick: Differentiating $y=Ce^x$ reproduces $y$ itself: $dy/dx=y$.

questions.q: In the linear differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$, if $Q=0$, the equation reduces to
options: an equation with no arbitrary constant
questions.explanation: With $Q=0$ it becomes $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-Py$, i.e. $\dfrac{dy}{y}=-P\,dx$, which is variable separable.
questions.trick: $Q=0$ makes a linear DE separable: $dy/y=-P\,dx$.

questions.q: The degree of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$ is
questions.explanation: Squaring both sides gives $\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2=1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$, a polynomial equation in the derivatives, so the degree is $2$ (not undefined).
questions.trick: Square both sides to clear the root, making it polynomial before reading the degree.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\tan x$ is
questions.explanation: Separating, $\dfrac{dy}{y}=\tan x\,dx \Rightarrow \ln|y| = -\ln|\cos x|+C \Rightarrow y = A\sec x$.
questions.trick: $dy/y=\tan x\,dx$ integrates to $\ln|\sec x|$, so $y=C\sec x$.

questions.q: If $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy$ and $y(0)=1$, then $y(1)=$
questions.explanation: Separating, $\ln y=x^2+C$; with $y(0)=1$, $C=0$, so $y=e^{x^2}$, giving $y(1)=e$.
questions.trick: Separate to $\ln y=x^2+C$, then exponentiate to get $y=Ae^{x^2}$.

questions.q: The integrating factor of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y\cot x=\sin2x$ is
questions.explanation: Here $P=2\cot x$, so $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int2\cot x\,dx}=e^{2\ln\sin x}=\sin^2x$.
questions.trick: $\int P\,dx$ with $P=n\cot x$ gives I.F.$=\sin^n x$ — a pattern to remember.

questions.q: For the homogeneous equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$, substituting $y=vx$ reduces it to
questions.explanation: With $y=vx$, $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{v}$, so $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{v}$, i.e. $v\,dv=\dfrac{dx}{x}$.
questions.trick: Substituting $y=vx$ often reduces to $v\,dv=dx/x$ — separate right away.

questions.q: A population grows at a rate proportional to its size, $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$. If it doubles every 5 years, then $k=$
questions.explanation: $P=P_0e^{kt}$; doubling gives $2=e^{5k}\Rightarrow 5k=\ln2\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{\ln2}{5}$.
questions.trick: Doubling-time formula: $k=\ln2/(\text{doubling time})$.

questions.q: The differential equation whose general solution is $y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-2x}$ is
questions.explanation: Differentiating twice, $y''=4Ae^{2x}+4Be^{-2x}=4y$, so $y''-4y=0$.
questions.trick: Exponent squared (here $2^2{=}4$) becomes the coefficient in $y''-4y=0$.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+\dfrac{2x}{y}=y$ is
questions.explanation: Here $P_1=2/y$, so $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int\frac{2}{y}dy}=y^2$. Then $xy^2=\int y^3\,dy=\dfrac{y^4}{4}+C$, so $x=\dfrac{y^2}{4}+\dfrac{C}{y^2}$.
questions.trick: $x$ as dependent variable: use I.F.$=e^{\int P_1dy}$, not the usual $x$-form.

questions.q: The particular solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=e^{-x}$ with $y(0)=0$ gives $y(1)=$
questions.explanation: I.F. $=e^x$; $(ye^x)'=1 \Rightarrow ye^x=x+C$. With $y(0)=0$, $C=0$, so $y=xe^{-x}$, giving $y(1)=\dfrac1e$.
questions.trick: Solve the linear DE fully first, apply $y(0)=0$, then evaluate at the target $x$.

questions.q: Which of the following differential equations is homogeneous?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{x+y}{x-y}$ is a function of $y/x$ alone (degree 0 in $x,y$), so it is homogeneous; the others mix terms of different degrees or have a constant term.
questions.trick: Check: can the RHS be written purely as a function of $y/x$?

questions.q: If $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+9y=0$ with $y(0)=2$ and $y'(0)=3$, then $y(\pi/6)=$
questions.explanation: $y=A\cos3x+B\sin3x$; $y(0)=A=2$, $y'(0)=3B=3\Rightarrow B=1$. At $x=\pi/6$: $y=2\cos(\pi/2)+\sin(\pi/2)=0+1=1$.
questions.trick: $y=A\cos3x+B\sin3x$; use $y(0)$ for $A$, $y'(0)/3$ for $B$.

questions.q: If $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}{x}$ and $y(1)=1$, then $y(e)=$
questions.explanation: With $y=vx$: $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1\Rightarrow v=\ln x+C$; $y(1)=1\Rightarrow v=1=C$. So $y=x(\ln x+1)$, giving $y(e)=e(1+1)=2e$.
questions.trick: After solving for $v$, back-substitute $y=vx$ and use the initial point for $C$.

questions.q: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\cot x=2\cos x$ is
questions.explanation: I.F. $=e^{\int\cot x\,dx}=\sin x$. Then $(y\sin x)'=2\cos x\sin x=\sin2x$, so $y\sin x=-\dfrac12\cos2x+C$.
questions.trick: I.F.$=\sin x$ turns the LHS into $d/dx(y\sin x)$ — recognise this pattern.

questions.q: The differential equation of the family of parabolas $y^2=4a(x-b)$, where $a,b$ are arbitrary constants, is
questions.explanation: Differentiating once: $2yy'=4a$. Differentiating again (RHS is constant): $2(y')^2+2yy''=0$, i.e. $yy''+(y')^2=0$.
questions.trick: Two constants: differentiate twice to eliminate both, landing on a 2nd-order DE.
